cultivar: Fenghuang Shui Xian, Mo Li Xiang strain
processing: Sun-withered, shaken overnight to a light-medium oxidation, fixed, rolled into long strips and lightly charcoal roasted; no jasmine flowers are involved, the aroma is the plant's own.
harvest_season: Spring, April into early May; an early-to-mid-season strain picked once, with occasional winter xue pian lots from lower gardens.
appearance_dry: Long, slender olive-green to brown strips with a clean jasmine smell.
appearance_wet: Long, soft yellow-green leaves with light red edges.
taste_profile: A clean jasmine aroma with no scenting behind it, a light-to-medium body with honeyed sweetness, a creamy softness and a cool, fresh finish.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, thin gaiwan, flash steeps; a slightly cooler kettle (95 °C) suits very lightly roasted lots. Drink the first five steeps and stop before it thins.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, spring tea lightly roasted and on sale from around June, with winter xue pian lots sold fresh in December. The light roast makes it a drink-young tea: best within a year, kept sealed and cool, and not aged.
description:
Mo Li Xiang, jasmine fragrance, is the Phoenix dancong that smells of jasmine without ever having met a jasmine flower: named on many lists of the ten classic aroma types, a long-leaf oolong from the Fenghuang Mountains above Chaozhou whose own leaf chemistry produces the scent that jasmine green tea gets from layering with blossoms.

That distinction is the first thing to say about it, because people assume scenting. Chinese jasmine tea is made by stacking tea with fresh flowers overnight, repeatedly; Mo Li Xiang dancong is made like every other dancong, from a selected single tree of the Fenghuang Shui Xian population propagated by cuttings, withered in the sun, shaken through the night, rolled into strips and charcoal roasted. The jasmine note is in the plant, and it shows most clearly when the oxidation and the roast are kept light, which is how makers treat it.

In the cup it is pale gold, with a clean, cool jasmine aroma, a honeyed sweetness, a soft, slightly creamy body and a fresh finish; it is lighter than Mi Lan Xiang and quieter than Ya Shi Xiang, which makes it a good tea for the afternoon or for a first meeting with dancong.

Brew it with the Chaozhou method, plenty of leaf, boiling or just-below-boiling water, instant pours, and take the first five steeps for what they are; it is not a long-running tea and extended steeps only thin it. It is also one of the few dancongs that holds up brewed in a pot for a minute.

It is sold by year with the village stated by serious sellers and should be drunk within the year, sealed and away from heat. It is a mid-priced strain and less widely planted than the honey and gardenia types, so it is more likely to be found with Chaozhou specialists than in general shops. If you enjoy it, Yu Lan Xiang is its gentle magnolia cousin and Ya Shi Xiang the louder honeysuckle one.
sources_note: Listed among the ten classic aroma types in Chaozhou sources; the mother-tree site is not stated because sources differ.
history:
Mo Li Xiang is one of the aroma types of Phoenix dancong rather than a tea with a recorded story of its own, and little is documented about its origin. It appears on a common Chaozhou list of ten aromas, but the list is a working convention: another version leaves jasmine out and names pomelo flower instead.

The jasmine note comes from the leaf and not from scenting.
